newsitem.title: USA: SEC drops probe of 1994 DC note offering - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: SEC drops probe of 1994 DC note offering - lawyer.

text.p: The SEC has closed its inquiry into whether District of Columbia officials adequately disclosed the city's financial problems when it sold $250 million in notes in late 1994, a city lawyer said on Tuesday.

"The Securities and Exchange Commission has advised counsel for the District that its investigation has been terminated and, as a result, no enforcement action will be recommended to the Commission," Ronald Liebman, outside counsel to the city, said in a telephone interview.

When the notes were sold through a syndicate led by Prudential Securities Inc, bond documents estimated a D.C. budget deficit at $492 million. Six weeks later, however, city officials placed the deficit at roughly $722 million.
SEC staff examined whether the city adequately disclosed Medicaid and other liabilities, Liebman said.

"I think its the right decision," Liebman said, of SEC's letter. "The SEC investigated the matter and determined that it was inappropriate to bring a case. That's what we told them from the very beginning. That's the right call."

Richard Sauer, assistant director of enforcement at SEC, said he had no comment on this specific matter. But he said, in general, a letter announcing the closure of a case should not automatically be read as an "exoneration" of the parties.
Liebman said SEC notified the city of its decision in a letter to Frederick Douglas of Leftwich & Douglas in Washington, co-counsel for D.C. in the matter.
